Fatal Effects of Intoxication in the þÿArmy In the year 1798, when the 07th Regiment then newly arrived and in garrison at Cape St. Nicholas Mole, St. Domingo, was ordered upon an expedition up the country, the troops previously to marching oil', were supplied with a full ration of spirits It was, as might have been foreseen, speedily consumed, and the men marching under a burning sun through a dry rocky country that furnished no water, fell down at almost every step. Nineteen actually died upon the road, and those who arrived at the end of the march, a distance of about twelve miles, were in a state of exhaustion that cannot be described. No one, even amongst the officers, who ventured so much as to taste their spirits, escaped with impunity.

aaataimMrs. A Tale of Mystery þÿ In 1734, the following circumstance took place in Lincolnshire : þÿ It was the wedding-day of Mr. and Mrs. Grilfin þÿ I mean the actual, not the anniversary wedding-duy ; and the jocond bridegroom, bride, and their guests, were assembled about noon in the drawing-room, when a servant entered, and said a gentleman had called and anxiously wished to sprcak to Mr. Griffin; that ho was waiting below stairs, and would not come up, because fie came upon particular business- Mr. G. begged his company to excuse him for a few minutes, and quitted the room. One hour elapsed þÿ no bridegroom ; two hours lie did not appear; three, four þÿ there were no indications of his return. The bride's mind misgave iicr, and the liymcniul guests

RTWsw » became much alarmed. The servants, one and all, declared they had seen their master and the gentleman who had so unexpectedly arrived, walk into the garden, whence they had not returned. Now, a high brick wall, in which there was no outlet, and over which no person could climb except by a ladder, enclosed the garden, which, when searched, was found empty ; whilst at the same time it was clear that Mr. Griffin and his friend "the gentleman" could not have walked back, and passed through the hall-door, without being, from its situation, seen and heard by the servants in the kitchen. Time, however, fled ; year after year passed over, and Mr. Grillin did not re-appear : no! þÿ and although his lady lived to be nearly ninety years of age, she never gained any tidings of the spouse thus so mysteriously spiritedaway. þÿ Lincolnshire Chronicle.

Origin of the Word Quiz; þÿ Very few words ever took such a run, or was saddled with so many meanings as this monosyllable : and however strange not one of otir 1< xicographers, from Bavley to Johnson, ever attempted an explanation, or gave a derivation of it. The reason is very obvious. It is hecause it has no meaning, nor is it derived frcm any language in the world ever known fr< in the Babylonish confusion to this day. \\ hen Richard Daly was patentee of the Irish theatres, he spent the evening of a Saturday in company with many of the wits and men of fashion of the day ; gambling was introduced, when the manager staked a large sum that lie would have spoken all through the principal streets in Dublin, by a certain hour next day, Sunday, a word having no meaning, and being derived from no þÿlanguage, wagers were laid and stakes deposited. Daly repaired to the theatre, and dispatched all the servants and supernumeraries with the word "Quiz," which they chalked on every door and shop window in town. Shops being shut all next day, every body going to and coming from their different places of worship saw the word, and every body repeated it, so that qu z was heard all through Dublin; the circumstance of so strange a word being on every door and window, caused much surprise, and ever since, should a strange story be attempted to he passed current, it draws forth the expression þÿ you are quizzing me,

Burnino op the Ship Eari. of Eli>on. þÿ Letters were yesterday received at Lloyd's from Fort l/ouis, Mauritius, dated the 25th of October, which gives the particulars of the destruction of the ship Ear! of Eldon by fire and the miraculous preservation of the crew. It appears that on the passage from Bombay to London, the Earl of Eldon caught fire on the 27th of September, in consequence of the cotton igniting, in lat. 9, 50, S. and long. 77. 22 E It was discovered at four a. m., and, notwithstanding every effort, by three p. m., the Captain (Theaker) was obliged to abandon the ship, the crew and passengers escaping in the boats with no more clothes than those they then had on. In this dreadfui situation they remained on the waters thirteen days, sailing in the boats a distance of 1,029 miles, until they arrived at the Isle of Rodriguez on the 10th of October, in a most deplorable state. They were very kindly received, and met with the most hospitable treatment from the inhabitants, who furnished them with food and raiment. They remained there nine days, and left in a small schooner with two of the boats. During the escape from the ship, one of the boats, on board which was Mr. Simpson and nine men was split by the sea in a gale of wind, and these were taken on board the long boat, which then contained 35 persons, while nine were in the small boat. The total number on board were nine passengers, an infant of four months old, three servants, and the crew, making 45. At the date of the

( From the Barbados Mercury, May 12.) JAMAICA. We regret to state that several cases of yellow fever have occurred in the (54th liegt. as well as on board some of the ships of war at Fort Royal. The Vestal, Captain Jones, and Dee, steamer, l.ieut Ramsay, have been towed out of the harbour the former vessel þÿ has lost her surgeon, a þÿmaster mate, s and a midshipman, from the effects of the fatal epidemic The 64th were removed from Fort Augusta to Park Camp on Wednesday evening. It is said that not more than three officers of the corps are fit for duty. We trust the change of climate will restore both officers and men to health.

We have much pleasure in extracting from the Nassau Royal Cazette of the s»t>th Feb. the following gratifying and pleasing accounts of the reception of the Commander and Officers of H M. (Ship the Forte, Commodore Fell, by the Governor and inhabitants of 11avannah. þÿ Such marks of attention and kindness between nations at peace cannot be but productive of the most beneficial results. We understand that the Commodore and Officers ot the Forte, entertain very grateful recollections of the kindness of bis Excellency the Captain General Tacon, as well as the other distinguished individuals who so magnificently and hospitably entertained them : Early on Thursday morning, a large ship appeared in the offing, which on approaching the anchorage opposite the town, was recognised by her broad pennant, as being his Maþÿjesty s ship Forte, Commondore Fell, from Jamaica ; but having on the previous evening read in a Kingston paper, that the Lord Bishop had embarked in tins ship for this part of his Diocese, we were led to suppose that his Lordship was on board. The Forte on anchoring was saluted from the Garrison guns, and it was soon discovered his Excellency Col. Colebrooke, the l.ieut. Governor, had arrived in her. IBs Excellency, accompanied by his private .Secretary and Commodore Pell, landed at the Ordinance wharf about eleven o'clock, where he was received by the Commandant, the officers of the garrison, and a guard of honor from the 2d West India Regiment, under salutes from the guns of the

Royal Artillery, at the saluting battery, and from those of the Nassau Artillery Company, formed on the abutment in front of the Public Buildings. From the wharf his Excellency proceeded to overnment House, where he was received by Mr. President i lunter, the President and members of his þÿMajesty sCouncil, and the Public officers ; when his Excellency w as sworn as Lieut. Governor and Commander in Chief of the colony ; immediately after w hich a salute was fired by the Royal Artillery, drawn up there for the purpose.

I he Forte being last from Havannah, we are informed, arrived there on the 18th instant, where she remained a few days for the purpose of communicating with the authorities, and landing some Spanish prisoners accused of having murdered the master of their vessel. Commodore Pell and the Lieut. Governor paid their respects to his Excellency the Captain General Tacon, a distinguished officer, who had been Captain General in Adalusia, and recently appointed to the government of 'uba. þÿ 1 1 is Excellency entertained them at dinner, and shewed them the most distinguished attention. The Captain General afterwards accepted an invitation from Commo-

dore Pell to dine on board the Forte ; a compliment the more marked as it was the first occasion on which a Spanish Governor and Captain General dined on board a Foreign ship. His Excellency expressed himself highly gratified by the manner he was received and entertained by the Commodore. The Commodore, the Lieut. Governor, and other officers, were also sumptuously entertained by Commodore Topete ; by the Count and Countess þÿO Reilly, where they met at dinner nearly sixty of the Spanish Nobility and Gentry, v ith their families. The entertainment was in elegant style They dined also w;th the English Consul, Mr. Tolir.e, and with Mr Tenant, cue of the principal English Merchants. On the evening before their departure, they attended a Grand Bull, which was specially given by th> members of the Philharmonic Society to the Commodore, where they met all die most distinguished families at that time in the Havana. The Hospitalities and attentions were proofs of a strong desire on the part of the Spanish Authorities, and the distinguished Society of the Capital, to manifest their good will towards the English. þÿ Herald, April. 17.)

We are very happy to learn that the ship Frances, Captain Heath, of the House of Messrs Higginson, Deane, As Scott, of this town, which vessel sailed for Liverpool, and put into Martinique on her way, in a leaky state, has received from the French naval commander, Admiral De Mackau, and the Governor, Vice Admiral Halgan, every attention which her situation demanded, and that the ship has been thus enabled to proceed onwards, on her destined voyage. As usual on such occasions, the port charges were remitted. This gratifying circumstance enables us to congratulate the two nations on the amity and good will which happily prevail beiweee them, and which it is our most \ ardent desire to see cultivated and promoted by such praiseworthy and noble acts as the one wo have been here called upon to notice. Barbados Mercury May 12,

We regret to have to announce the death of Sir Peter Parker, from a dr eadful attack of small pox. The prevalence of this terrible mallady at present lias caused a feeling of alarm on all sides from the mortality which has hitherto attended it and the unusual severity with which it has attacked persons of all classes and ages. The death of Sir Peter Faiker, who was but a few days since in perfect health, lias plunged his family and numerous friends in the severest affliction. þÿ Glasgow Courier.

We have pleasure in noticing the great blessing we have had in the abundance of rain which has tallen since an early hour of yesterday morning. From the appearance of the clouds we should hope it is general throughout the Island. þÿ Barbadian May 13.

Considerable interest is attached to the movements of our squadron in the Mediteranean. It will be seen, by a paragraph under our London head, that despatches had reached Malta on the 3d ult. from Lord Ponsonby at Constantinople, in consequence of which Sir Josias Rowley set sail on the 7th with six line of battle ships, three frigates, and some smaller craft. Nothing has transpired as to their destination, of a positive character, but it is believed that they are bound for the Dardanelles, as reports were prevalent at Malta, of serious disturbances having occurred in Constantinople, which rendered it advisable for a British force to make a demonstration in that quarter. But as we have already mentioned, there is nothing certain known, cither as to the route, or as to the object ot this expedition, þÿ Glasgow Courier, March 12.

SUBLIME SERMON. A young Prussian marched as a volunteer against the French in 1813, and had been made an officer, þÿi revious to taking arms ho had been a student of theology and is now a minister. On the morning of the battle at Lcipzic, the commander of his battalion called upon him to preach to the soldiers. The usual scaffold of drums was formed ; the regiment was placed on a bill, the view7 from which extended over a large part of the field of the largest battle ever þÿrecorded the giant battle, as it olten has been termed. þÿ It is easy to imagine ho- . the preacher lelt when he stood on bis elevation, and looked on his brethren in arms, and on the extensive plain which was soon to dri.ik the blood ot the brave in torrents. 11c began, þÿ brethren, warriors þÿ there is the enemy of our country þÿ there is Cod þÿ (pointing towards heaven) þÿ pray þÿ! He could say no more. The whole congregation in arms prayed in silence, when the distant thunder c artillery called them to their martial duty, and gave the signal that the murderous contest was beginning which raged three days, and decided the fate of Europe.

INFLUENCE OF THE MOON. In considering the climate of tropical countries, the influence of the moon seems to be entirely overlooked ; and surely, if the tides of the vast ocean are raised from their fathomless bed by lunar power, it is not too much to assert that the tides of the atmosphere are liable to a similar influence ; this much is certain, that iu the low lands of tropical countries no attentive observer of nature will fail to w itness the power exercised by the moon over the seasons, and also over animal and vegetable nature. þÿ As regards the latter, it may be stated that there are certainly thirteen springs and thirteen autumn? in Dernarara in the year ; for so many times does the sap ol trees ascend to the branches and descend to the roots. For example, the waliaba (a resinous tree, common in the Dernarara woods, somewhat resembling mahogany,) if cut down in the dark, a few days before the new moon, it is one of the most durable woods in the world lor house-building, posts, &c. ; in that state, attempt to split it. and, with the utmost difficulty, it would be riven in the most jagged, unequal manner that can be imagined ; cut down another waliaba that grew within a few yards of the former, at full moon, and the tree can be easilv split into the finest smooth shingles of any desired thickness, or into staves for making casks ; but, in this state, applied to house-building purposes, it speedily decays. Again : bamboos, a thick as a þÿman a s rm, are sometimes used for paling,

&c. ; if cat at the dark moon they will endure for ten or twelve years : if at full moon, they will be rotten in two or three years thus it is with most, if not all, the forest trees. Of the effects of 1 lie moon on animal life, very many instances could be cited I have seen in Alrica the newly-littered young perish in a few hours, at the þÿmother side, s if exposed to the rays of the tull moon ; fish became rapidly putrid, and meat, if left exposed, incurable or unpreservable by salt ; the mariner, heedlessly sleeping on the deck, becoming afflicted with nyctolopia, or night blindness, at times the face hideously swollen if exposed during sleep to the þÿmoon rays, s the maniac's paroxysms renewed with fearful vigour at the full and change, and the cold damp chill of the ague supervening on the ascendancy of this apparently mild yet powerful luminary. Let her influence over this earth be studied þÿ it is more powerful than is generally known, þÿ History of the British Colonies . Martin's

DEATH OF THE PRINCE AUGUSTUS OF PORTUGAL, (From the Falmouth Packet, April 4.) It is with feelings of unfeigned regret that we announce the death of this amiable Prince, which event took place at Lisbon, at twenty minutes past two þÿo clock on Saturday afternoon last, the 28th of March. His Majesty had suffered some slight inconvenience for a few days from cold, which, ultimately, produced quinsey, and this complaint, baffling the skill of his medical attendants, terminated ftftally, to the great sorrow of his bereaved widow, the court, and the inhabitants of Lisbon, to whom his majesty had endeared himself by the urbanity of his manners and by his attention to the interests of Portugal, to promote which, in every possible way, he manifested the utmost anxiety.

When nearly under the line, west of þÿWashington s Island, they perceived a whale of an extraordinary size. The boats were all immediately lowered, and to make the capture more sure, they were manned with the whole crew: the cook's mate alone remained at the helm, and the ship lay to. 'I'he monster, as it peaceably floated on the surface of the water, was eagerly followed and harpooned. (In feeling the stroke of the weapon, it lashed its tail with fury, and the boat nearest it was obliged to dart with all

speed out of the wav to avoid instant destruction. The whale then turned its vengeance on the ship, swam several times round her with prodigious noise, and then struck her so violently on the hows, that the þÿcook s mate could compare the client of the blow only to the shock of an earthquake. The fish disappeared, but the leak the ship had sprung sunk her in five minutes with all that she contained, ller solitary guardian was with difficulty saved. The crew were now left in four open boats, several þÿweeks voyage from the nearest land, and with no provisions but the little biscuit they happened to have with them. After a long discussion on the best course to be pursued, they separated. Two of the boats steered for the Washington or Marquesas isles ; and the other two, with the captain in on i of then, towards the south, for the island of Juan Ferna idez The former have not since been h >rd of, but the latter were a fortnight a' erwaids picked up by a vessel, when the captain and four only of his men were found utve; the other ten had died of hunger. and their corpses had a Horded nourishment to tiie survivors. þÿ Kotzebue's Voyages.

STATE OF CANADA. We are sorry to observe the state to which internal faction is reducing this flourishing Country. A House divided against itself can' not stand, nor can the Canadas long continue to be valuable to the country, if they are to be divided by national feeling as well as local interests. The inhabitants of Lower Canada are chiefly descendants of the old colonists, to whom their laws and customs were guaranteed at the conquest, and are so injurious to the future welfare of the country, that they ought to be abrogated, giving them compensation for any loss that might tic sustained ; whatever may be done, it is evident that unless it is done speedily a serration of the two provinces must take place, and then both will fall an easy prey to the Americans on the slightest rupture with the United States. Such an insult as that offered to the Representative of His Majesty, we believe has never been heard of under any Government ; but it is to be hoped the officer administering that of Lower Canada will dissolve the Assembly and refuse to call another until His þÿMajesty s pleasure is known. The house of Assembly of Lower Canada has commenced the session with unexampled tyranny and violence: indeed, every mail brings us some fresh act of violence and outrage upon the feelings and liberties of British subjects. The first act was to expunge from the minutes the speech from the throne, delivered at the close of last session. The next act was to address the Governor, demanding

that the elective principle be extended to the Legislative Council, the body which is analagous to the House of Lords, a demand which all know cannot be yielded without violating the fundamental character of the British constitution. England has given to Canada her own constitution, and beyond this she cannot go. The House next distinguished itself by seizing and sending to the common jail Mr. Jessup, the Collector of the Customs, an officer holding his commission from the crown; this outrage on personal liberty was effected on the charge of contempt of the House in refusing to give up certain papers and documents in his department, and which he dared not to do without an order from the Governor. In short, the progress of tyranny has become so alarming that no person is safe We again urge our fellow subjects to lose not an hour, in proceeding to the foot of the Throne, and also laying before the Imperial Parliament the long list of grievances under which they groan. Let them without delay call their British brethren in England for succor, and show them the hideous despotism under which they labour þÿ a despotism, the cruellest of all, the despotism, of ignorance, inflicted on them by men who cannot write their own names. þÿ Jamaica Despatch.

Lord Brougham. þÿ On Monday evening Lord Brougham presented a petition against the stamp duty on newspapers His Lordship having been frightened by the consequences of his lengthy commentary on the Canada petition, imposed on himself a sort of moral straitwaistcoat, and when he presented a petition on the following day, abstained even from mentioning the nature of the petition, or the name of the petitioner. But this restiaint could not of course belong endured. His Lordship, who certainly would never have passed through the Pythagorean ordeal of a nine þÿyears silence, and whose talent for retention is on a par with that of the celebrated wife of Midas, has burst the trammels of his selfimposed controul, and on Monday night accompanied a petition with a very long speech. We hardly know whether we should congratulate his Lordship on the recovery of his liberty. He evidently thinks that he is a perfect master of the subject which he discusses, and we suppose he will not put much trust in our assertion, when we assure him that he knows every little about the þÿmatter. Population can only increase and flourish in proportion to the security of property and person. Mankind will not willingly select that place for an abode where the latter is in constant danger, either from defective laws, or the tyranny of rulers ; nor will the labourer the artisan, or the man of talent devote time, physical energies, genius and intelligence in amassing wealth, which they feel conscious niay be wrested from them at any moment at the point of the þÿdespot sbayonet or by the knife of the bandit. Hence arises the inertness of the poor working classes, the natives of such places, who limit their exertions simply to living from hand to mouth; as also the inactivity of the man of talent, who either suffers his genius to sleep or emigrates to some moie happy shore, where he may securely reap the fruits of his application. The annals of history prove to us that in every country in the world, population and industry have kept pace with the justice and freedom of public laws and institutions ; and the most prosperous period, as regards former, has always been simul- the taneous with the flourishing era of the latter.

On the morning of the 2d April, 1 1 is Maþÿjesty schooner s Skipjack, on her passage from Belize to Port Royal, with despatches, observed a strange sail on her weather bow ; on nearing her, she made her out to be a brig running to the westward, under all sail, and on the Skipjack's tacking to close with her, she immediately took in her studding sails, and hauled to the wind. The Skipjack then made all sail in chase, and wishing to discover her character shewed her colours, when the brig hoisted a Spanish ensign and penant, and fired two guns to leeward. On getting within shot, the Skipjack fired a gun a head of the brig, but observing her shortening sail, and preparing to engage, fired into her. which she immediately returned with round grape and double-headed shot. She continued engaging the Skipjack at close quarter, for two hours, after which she made all sail with the view to escape. The Skipjack following her, and keeping up a heavy tire with her long gun, at half past K) i\ m. she surrendered, and proved to be the Spanish brig þÿ þÿMarte, formerly a man of war pierced for 18 guns, but mounting six Congreve 18 pounders, and two long 12's, with a crew ot 56 men, and a cargo of 445 slaves, out of 7140 originally embarked she þÿ had one seaman and seven slaves killed, and six seamen and eleven slaves wounded, and was likewise dreadfully cut up in her rigging and sails She has been sent to the llavanna under charge of Mr. Marrett.and Lieut. Further particulars of the capture of the Spanish Slaver by H. M. Schooner Skipjack, Lieut Usher. In addition to the account which has already been given of the capture of the Spanish Slaver Marte, we are enabled to give the following particulars : þÿ The Marte was discovered by the Skipjack about 50 miles to the northward of the Grand Caymanas, but, from her appearance, was taken for a merchantman ; but on the Skipjack tacking for the purpose of ascertaining her character, the brig immediately took in her studding sails, and hauled close to the wind, being then about five miles to windward of the Skipjack This manoeuvre excited suspicion, and all sail was made in chase. On the Skipjack shewing her colours, a large Spanish ensign and penant were displayed from the brig, firing two guns to leeu-ard ; and she soon afterwards hauled down the colours. On nearing the brig, the Skipjack fired a shot a-head ; and on seeing the vessel shorten sail and prepare for action, a fire was immediately opened at her at about a quarter ol a mile distance. The Skipjack, after continuing the action for þÿ oine time, wore to avoid being raked, and renewed the action on the starboard lack. þÿ After the engagement had lasted lor two hours, the brig made all sail, endeavouring to escape. Tiie Skipjack immediately gave chace, keeping up a heavy fire from her long tom, which the brig returned from her stern-chasers þÿ The wind falling light, the Skipjack got out her sweeps, and neared the chace fast At

half past 10 p. m , the Skipjack running up in the most determined manner to board tne brig, a light was exhibited ; and on Lieutenant Usher demanding if they had struck, the instant reply was yes ! yes ! yes III (or God's sake þÿdon fire. t The vessel was then taken possession of, and found to be the Marte, formerly a national vessel, pierced for 18 guns ; 'but only mounting six Congreve 18 pounders, and two long twelves, with a crew of 56 men ! In consequence of the number of prisoners on board the Skipjack, Lieut Usher proceeded to the Grand Caymanas, where he landed and placed thirty-four of the crew in a place of security ; in which service he was most zealously aided by Mr. Drayton, the senior Maths rate, and llr Thompson, the Special Magistrate þÿ The prize was sent on to the llavanna, in charge of Mr. Marett, the first mate of the Skipjack þÿ a very old and meritorious

In this gallant affair we are happy to state that not an officer or man were injured on board the schooner ; although her sails and running rigging suffered very considerably. The loss on board the brig was one sailor, and seven slaves killed ; one sailor, and eleven slaves wounded. The brig suffered much in her hull, rigging, and sails ; the latter were completely riddled bv round and grape. Mo less than one hundred shot had been fired from the schooner, at her huge antagonist, before she surrendered ! ! The schooner mounted only the long tom, with a compliment of men and officers of only 37, including seven boys ! The brig of 450 tons, with 8 guns, and a crew of 56 men !! The gallantry displayed in this action is highly creditable to Lieutenant Usher, his officers, and men ; and exhibit, in the most glow ing colours, the determined spirit of our gallant tars in the execution of their duty. þÿ We cordially congratulate the crew of this little vessel on their brilliant success; and have no doubt that the gallant conduct and bravery displayed on this occasion, will be duly appreciated by His Majesty's Government. Lieutenant Usher is þÿ a chip of that old þÿblock, JSir Thomas Usher, K. C. A retail dealer of respectability has handed to us a counterfeit English shilling, which circulated here for a quarter dollar, and was received by him in change in the course of business. This base coin bears the effigies of Geor. III. and the dale is 1816; on tlie reverse side are the royal arms sui mounted by the crow n and encircled by the garter with its appropriate motto. The material of which this spurious piece of money is fabricated is copper, which has been thinly washed, not plaied, with silver: the execution of it is inferior to the genuine coin, a circumstance easily to be discovered upon a close examination. especially in the line of the forehead on one side, and in the embroidered end of the garter on the other. The whole appearance of the coin is much too new for a piece of money that has been circulating for nineteen years, and the prominent parts are less worn down than the true money ol the same date. The counterfeit lies at our office for the inspection of anv one w ho may be desirous of examining it. We shall be hnppv to be the means of warning the public against any other similar counterfeits, if those who discover them will enable us to do so. We understand that several spurious half crowns (5s 7£d currency) arc going about, but our endeavours to obtain possesion of, or to get a sight of one, for the purpose of examination, have been hitherto unsuccessful.

Notwithstanding the ominous predictions ot our inability to carry on the Government, I own to yon that do entertain the greatest confidence that those predictions will not be verified, and that the representatives of the country will not refuse to give to the King's Ministers a fair trial. Great cheering. A few weeks only can elapse before the experiment will be made, i am not alarmed at the lists that are published, dividing the Members of Parliament into þÿ Conservatives and þÿ Reformers. I cannot but think that many ot those, who are classed as Reformers, entertain opinions not far different from my own; and every hour that passes will, 1 doubt not, increase the disposition to take a calmer view of the principles upon which we propose to act. Cheers If the public and the Representatives of this country are convinced that we are desirous of maintaining our national institutions, and of impioving them, with a view to their maintenance, 1 do not believe that they will lend themselves to any factious opposition to the King's Government. Great cheering. The people England of are anxious, 1 believe, to preserve in their full integrity the prerogatives of their ancient Monarchy. They arc anxious to maintain the irce and independent action of every branch of the Legislature; they are anxious to maintain the Church and its connection with the state, less for any civil or secular object, than because they believe the maintenance of the Established Church to be the best security for

the maintenance of that faitli w hich they profess, and the surest bulwark against inti lelity on the one hand, and fanaticism on the other. They will support the Church on high grounds of religious feeling and principle, in which, even many, who do not conform to all the doctrines of the church, may cordially and zealously concur. This object, 1 for one, a n determined to maintain. Rapturous applause. But, it is quite consistent with that object to relieve anv real grievance, and to remove any civil disadvantage under which those who do not concur in the doctrines of the Established Church may labour. My opinion is that, with that course, coupled with a sincere desire to promote rational and and well matured improvement, the people of England will he content ; nay more, that of that course they will cordially approve. þÿ As for myself, whatever may be the result. 1 regard it without any feelings of anxiety or apprehension. 1 have no object of personal ambition to gratify, and whatever else I may lose, I cannot lose the consolation of having acted on a sense of public duty at a period of great difficulty. If 1 succeed, I shall have the satisfaction of thinking that 1 have succeeded against great obstacles and amidst the most confident predictions of failure. I believe that I shall stocked! Thunders of applause. I have that confidence in the success of good inteittions; that 1 believe a majority of the Representatives of England will he satisfied with the measures which I shall propose,

and that they will lend their support and co-operation in carrying them into effect. þÿ paper. Cheers. But, gentlemen, if I am mistaken þÿ if. after having exerted myself to the utmost in that great cause in which I am engaged þÿ if. having nothing to upbraid mvself with, I shall notwithstanding fail, then 1 do assure you, so far as mv personal feelings are þÿ orioorned, I shall relinquish the powers, the emoluments, and distinctions of office with anv toolings rather than those of mortification and regret. Great cheering. I shall find ample compensation for the loss of office. 1 shall return to pursuits quite as congenial to mv taste and feelings as the cares and labours of office. I shall feel that the arigrv contentions and collisions of political life, will but bind me the more to this place, not. indeed, the place of my nativity, but dearer to me i list of debts of honour and honesty ; and to than the place of mv nativity þÿ by every day recollection and association, and by the formation of those friendships, which have remained uninterrupted to this hour. I shall re turn here, to do what good 1 can in a more limited sphere, and with humbler powei of ac-

Lord Stanley, having been elected Lord Rector of Glasgow College, made, according to custom, at his inauguration, a pretty lengthy speech, in which occur the following allusions to passing political events : þÿ þÿ In me von will lira! one ready to assist in removing all blemishes and deformities from the best and holiest institutions of the country, with the most uncompromising zeal þÿ while, at the same time, 1 will oppose, with all the might and energy 1 am capable, those whose measures, whose objects, and whose intentions þÿ are not to reform, hut to destroy. Would to God that that great man, whose name I can never mention but with the profoumlest respect and reverence, had been enabled lo remain in office to guide the helm of government by his steady and skilful hand þÿ unmoved by tho praise ot his friends or the spleen of las opponents! That man was the true patriot, the strenuous defender of the privileges of the Crown, the rights of the people and the aristocracy. But 1 now sincerely trust that, into whatever hands the helm of the State may come, no man will ever conceive that he can check the spirit of improvement, ol inquiry, and investigation, which must now go on. This will never do the wishes of the þÿ people must not be put aside þÿ they must be met bv a fair and determined spirit to do just what is right, and no more. The machine must move onward for good oi evil þÿ for it cannot he stopped ; like the fire, it may purify, it properly guided by a skilful hand ; hut if it

should he impetuously and recklessly accelerated, destruction and overwhelming wreck must be the inevitable consequences. 1 1 is will he a glorious destiny who knows how io direct and turn into their proper channel (the spirit of the age) the energies of the people, and to conduct with propriety at this period, the Government of this great nation; but if he shall imagine himself capable of stemming and abruptly resisting its force onwards, lie vviil be swept along with the torrent. I trust that the Ministry whoever they be, will act with prudence in this most important þÿcrisis.

CAREER OF LOUIS PHILIPPE. A French paper gives the following epitome of the career of King Louis Philippe : Louis Philippe, was born (he Cth of ( Ictober 173, at first Puke of Valois, then the Puke of Chartres, then General Egalite, then Puke of Orleans, then King of the French. The life of this Prince is filled with contrasts; Jie is one of the most striking examples of the vicissitudes of human thought, in 1793, he signed himself Louis Philippe Egalite; his to' misfortune, a French Prince, in 1810, he reclaimed this title at Tarrogonia; he was proud ol it. in 1814, he made use of it in 1830, to seat hiniselfon the first throne in the world, iu 1798, he destroyed the iron cage of Mount

St. Michael. In 1833, he had the cells of this abbey rebuilt and erected it into a state prison ; in 1792, he saved, in Vendome, a soldier who was drowning; in 1834. his constables fire at, and kill a man who is swimming for his life; in 1830, he declares himself more a republican than Lafayette, and is oliended at the insolence of Pupont þÿl Eure, who pretends to think himself more of a republican than he is ; in 1833, his government establishes the condition of siege and the rule of the sword to defend the monarchical system. A republican soldier under ihe tri-colored Hag, he signalized himself at Jemmappes and Valmy, and ilien swears allegiance and homage to his lord, king, and master, l.ot.is XV1I1., and bedecks himself with the white tieur de lis. up to the day when he again takes an oath to live and die lor the honor and in defence ol the colors for which he had fought in his youth Verily, when historians shall have recorded all tlu acts and movements of Louis Philippe, the record will he an enigma to posterity, who will have diiiiculty in believing that the last forty years have been enriched with but one Louis Philippe of Orleans The French w riter concludes with the following ominous announcement. On the 6th of October, 1835, this Prince will be 62 years of age, the greatest ever attained by any member of his race and name.

A Zoological Mystery. þÿ On one of ins expeditions Linnaeus was, or imagined himself to have been, stung by a venetnous worm, said to be not uncommon in some parts of Sweden. However this may be, he was seized with a violent disorder which threatened the extinction of life, more especially as he had removed lar into the country, where medical assistance could not he readily procured. Tnis accident, instead of diminishing his zeal, tended to increase his desire of becoming more acquainted with the lower orders ol animals. In a work which he subsequently published, this singular worm, the existence ol which, however, is still doubtful, is thus described by him : þÿ It occurs in the extensive turly marshes of Bothnia, in the northern parts of Sweden. Falling from the atmosphere, frequently upon ihe bodies of men and animals, it instantly penetrates them with the most intense pain, so as to produce death from agony, within a quarter of an hour. I myself was smitten by it, at Lund, in 1728. I have not seen the animal unless in a dried state. It seems in its properties to he allied to the chaolic animal. By what means it rises into the air, whence it falls during the interval between the summer and winter solstice, no one has explained þÿ." Lives of Zoologists.

He has employed the director of Ponls ct-Chussees of our town to draw out the plans, so that the buildings may be commenced in three months from this time, wdicn his Lordship will return to Cannes. It has given great satisfaction in our neighbourhood that so honorable a personage has become one of our landed proprietors. þÿ Le Toulonnais.

In the midst of much prosperity, and when the colonists were exulting in their good fortune, the town of Port Royal, in Jamaica, into which the wealth of the buccaneers had been poured, and on whose shores their crimes and wickedness had been felt, was, by the awful interposition of Providence, suddenly destroy- I ed, and its inhabitants instantly engulfed in so much depravity, forever! On the th of the earthquake which entombed the scene of . June, 14112, at mid day, while the Governor and Council were sitting, and the wharfs were loaded with merchandize and rich spoil, a roar . . was heard in tne distant mountains, and reverberated through the valley to the beach, where the sea suddenly arose, and in an instant stood live fathoms deep, where a moment before were displayed the glittering treasures of Peru and Mexico ; in some places the earth opened wide and swallowed whole houses, which were again, perhaps, thrown upwards by the violent concussion of the sea ; in others, many individuals were swallowed up to the neck, and the earth then closing strangled them ; the Swan frigate was earned over the tops of the sunken houses, and afforded a providential escape to many persons, and of the whole town, perhaps the richest spot in the world, not more than two hundred houses of the Ibrt were left. The whole island felt severely the shock ; in some parts mountains were riven, in others connected, the outline of every thing was changed, and the entire sur-

face of the island considerably subsided ; many thousand persons were destroyed in the overwhelming of Port Royal, the ruins of which are still visible in clear weather, from the surface of the ocean, beneath w hich they lie.

INFLUENCE or Ml SIC ON THE MINO, Of the solace of music, nay more, of its influence upon melancholy, I need not look for evidenc e in the universal testimony of antiquity, nor remind such an audience of its recorded effect upon the gloomy distemper of the perverse mind of Saul. I myself have witnessed its power to mitigate the sadness of seclusion, in a case where mv loyalty as a good subject, and my best feelings as a mam were more than usually interested in the restoration of my patient ; and I also remember its salutary operation in the case of a gentleman in Yorkshire many years ago, who was first stupificd, and afterwards became insane upon tbe sudden loss of all his property. This gentleman could hardly be said to live þÿ he merely vegetated, for he was motionless until pushed, and did not speak to, nor notice any body in the house, for nearly four months. The first indication of a return of any sense appeared in his attention to music played in the street. This was observed, the second time he heard it, to have a more decided force in arousing him from his lethargy ; and induced bv this good omen, the sagacious humanity of his superintendent offered him a violin. He seized it eagerly, and amused himself with it constantly. After six weeks, hearing the rest of the patients of the house pass by his door to their common room, he accosted þÿthem. " Good morning to you all, gentlemen, I am quite well, and desire I may accompany you." In two mouths more, he was dismissed cured.

SSK THE THEATRE. Professor Griscom, of New-York, in a report on the causes of vice and crime in that city, three years ago, made the following statement " Among the causes of vicious excitement in our city, none appear to be so powerful in their operation as theatrical amusements. The number of boys and young men who have become determined thieves, in order to procure the means of obtaining introductions to the theatres and circuses, would appal the feelings of every virtuous mind, could the whole truth be laid open to them. " In the case of the feeble sex, the evil is still greater i a relish for the amusements of the theatre, without the means of indulgence, becomes too often a motive for listening to the first suggestions of the seducer, and thus prepares the unfortunate captive of sensuality for the haunts of infamy, and a total destitution of all that is valuable in the mind and character of woman." During the progress of the most ferocious revolution which ever shocked the face of heaven, theatres, in Paris alone, multiplied from six to twenty-five. Now, one of two conclusions follows from this: either the spirit of the times produced the institutions, or the institutions cherished the spirit of the times : and this will certainly prove that they are either the parents of vice, or the offspring of it. The infidel philosopher Rosseau, declared himself to be of opinion, that the theatre is, jn all cases, a school of vice. Though he had himself written for the stage, yet, when it was

proposed to establish a theatre in the city of Geneva, he wrote against the proposal with zeal and great force, and declared, that every friend of pure morals ought to oppose it. Sir John Hawkins, in his " Life cf Dr. Johnson," observes. þÿ " Although it has been said of plays, that they teach morality, and of the stage, tiiat it is the mirror of human life, these assertions arc mere declamation, and ha ve no foundation in truth and experience. On the contrary, a playhouse, and the regions about it, are the very hot-beds of vice." Archbishop Tillotson, after some pointed an i forcibly reasoning against it, pronounces the playhouse to be ' the devil's chapel,' a 4 nursery of licentiousness and vice,' and ' a recreation which ought not to be allowed among a civilized, much less a christian people.' Collier solemnly declares his persuasion, 4 that nothing had done more to debauch the age in which he lived, than the stage poets and the playhouse ' Sir Mathew Hale, having in earlv life, experienced the pernicious effects of attending the theatre, resolved, when he came to London, never to see a play again, and to this resolution he adhered through life. Even the heathen philosopher, Plato, understood the mischievous tendency of theatres: þÿ 4 Plays,' he says, 4 raise the passions, and perverts the use of them, and are, of course, dangerous to morality.'

THOMAS, SATURDAY JULY 18, 1835 þÿ oo þÿ033 By private letters received in this Island, we are sorry to perceive that a new calamity has befallen the Republic of Venezuela. þÿ The results of our inquiries is. that f<>r some Some military Chieftains not satisfied with the third part of their pay, out of service, and anxious for money and great employments, had succeeded through the inferior (Jllicers to seduce the small garrison of Caracas, consistin" of a Battalion of 400 men. The Revolu- O ti< >n broke out in the night, from the 7th to the 8th instant, when the Conspirators took possession of the Park of Artillery Military Stores, and arrested the President Doctor Jose V a it gas, in his own residence. A notorious bad Character named Carujo, (the same person whoassassinated in Bogota Mr. Eiikglhson, the aid de camp of Bolivak) was at the head of the Band of Soldiers, and tried (showing his prepared Pistols,) to compel the President to abdicate, which was scornfully and (irmly refused. (From the I Uc.vt Indian of Thursday ) Much alarm lias been created amongst some nervous people in town, in consequonce of an article which appeared in the Globe of Monday last, and which, if suflered to pass without contradiction, may extend to the neighbouring colonies and put the commercial and shipping interest to unnecessary loss aud inconveii.i nee, in consequence of the establishment of special quarantine regulations. 1 he Globe states that his Majesty's steamer Flamer was prevented conveying the mails per Kenard to Jamaica, in consequence of her olicers and crew being attacked with fever. This is perfectly true. But remarks arc afterwards made as to the steamer lying at anchor "to windward of alt the shipping in Carlisle Hay I" and a great deal more is said about Quarantine Laws, applying to the Governor, and so foith. Now, il the Editor ol the Globe had given himself the trouble to inquire into the matter, as we have done, he might have saved many persons from sutlering under unnecessary apprehensions; for, on reading his paper, who would think otherwise than that the demon of cholera morbus, yellow fever, or some oilier contageous disease, reigned on board the Flame r > We have the satisfaction
to state that the sickness was by no means of an infectious nature, but arose from local causes, and was not likely to extend to persons who had not been a considerable time on hoard the vessel.

time past, the F lamer had been in a leaky state, and in consequence of the quantity of coals which she carries, it was impossible for the leak to he got at ; consequently, in so confined a place as the hold of the vessel, and particularly under the boilers, the sea water acting on the coal, generated a noxious and poisonous gas, from which the dreadtul scourge, which has afflicted the officers and crew, originated. Having accounted for the cause of the sickness, we proceed to state what steps have been taken by persons in authority. His Excellency the Governor did not need to be reminded bv tfie Globe what his duty was in this respect : he had not lost a moment in inquiring most minutely into the circumstances cf the case. The Senior Naval Officer, Captain Macausland, had been with Ids Excellence, and had informed him that he had ordered a medical inquiry, the result of which had been such as wc have already stated. The surviving officers and crew being now convalescent, and the Flamer having been reinforced bv ten men from the Cruiser , sailed this day for English Harbour, Antigua, whi re she will be hove down and repaired. The Cruiser accompanied the steamer in order to render any assistance that may be required. Egypt, and has not abated in Lower Egypt. Alexandria is almost a desert, having lost, by death and emigration, two-thirds of its population. Meheniet Ali. who has personally a great dread of the plague, is said to intend to leave the country for a time. The cases at Constantinople are few, and no fears are felt that the disorder will spread. The north of European Turkey is free, but in Bosnia and part of Servia there is a malignant small pox, to which many grown up persons in particular fall victims. El.Ol'EMENT. ( From the Age ) The fashionable world have had a week's amusement in conjecturing, debating, approving, or censuring the conduct of all the parties interested in this very extraordinary affair. Sir Colquhoun Grant had long been aware that the young lady's fortune was an attractive object to numerous needy Captains, and had therefore adopted precautionary measures, Mr. Brinsley Sheridan had the good fortune first to meet the young lady at the house of his sister, the Hon. Mrs Norton; and that fascinating and clever woman very naturally did all she could to aid her brother suit. The matter was cautiously broken to Sir C. Grant, who as cautiously immediately forbade M r. B. Sheridan's visits. In this state matters remained when Sir Colquhoun Grant left London to attend to his election for Poole, leaving strict orders that no gentlemen visitors, except his brother, were to be admitted in his absence. On Friday last, about one o'clock Mrs Norton called, and took the young lady out for a drive in the Parks ; and being there, by some unaccountable accident, her brother, Mr. Brinsley Sheridan, was there al o, and being there, could do no less than gallantly renew his attentions to Miss Grant. Of course he obtained a scat in the same carriage. From the Park they drove to another sister of Mrs. Norton's. Lady Seymour. Here a scene occurred, which ended in Mr. Brinsley Sheridan borrowing from his friend, Col. Bentinck, of the Guards, the use of histravellingcarriage, which had just driven up, of course by accident.

There was now no impediment to immediate elopement but a wardrobe and money. The kind sister supplied this between them, and in addition furnished a lady's maid. Miss Grant wrote a note to her own waiting woman, by way of ruse, directing her to proceed with her wardrobe to Dover. All the preliminaries thus arranged, the parties popped into their carriage, and weie very soon in full swing for Gretnagreen, where they arrived and were married on the following Sunday The stories about the young lady 's fortune are, lor the most part, gross exaggerations she has not any thing like forty or twenty thousand pounds at h r own disposal on coming of age, but she has the unalienable right of (3,000/ . per annum on the death of her father. At present Sir C Grant is exceedingly wroth, and tin atens proceedings against all parties for abduction ; he has also stated bis determination of breaking up his establishment, and going abroad, fully resolved not to be reconciled. We hope, however, he will forget and forgive ; for, after all, Brinsley Sheridan is a dashing good looking fellow, and the lady might have done worse.

These peopled the earth as it was, not before the general deluge, but before some convulsion long prior to that event bud overwhelmed the countries then dry, and raised others then from the bottom of the sea. la these curious inquiries wo are conversant not merely with the world before the flood, but with a world which, before the flood, was covered with water, and which, in far earlier ages, bad been the habitation of birds, and beasts, and reptiles We are carried as it were, several worlds back, and we reach a period when all was water, and slime and mud ; and the waste without either men or plants, gave resting place to enormous beasts like lions, and elephants, and river horses, while the water was tenanted with lizards, the size of a whale, sixtv or seventy feet lone, J o» and by others with huge eyes, having shields ol solid bone to protect tliem, and glaring from a neck ten feet in length ; and the air was darkened by flying reptiles covered w ith scales, opening the jaws of the crocodile, and expanding wings armed at the tips with the claws of the leopard.

Di el with a Bag. þÿ Two gentlemen, one a Spaniard and the other a German, who were recommended by their birth and services to the Emperor Maximilian II., both courted liis daughter, the fair Hclcuc Scharlcquin. in

marriage. This prince, after a long delay, one day informed them, that es;e< ming them equally, and not being able to bestow a preference, be should leave it to the force and address of the claimants to decide the question. He did not mean, however, to risk the loss of one or the other, or perhaps of both. He could not, therefore, permit them to encounter with offensive weapons, but bad ordered a large bag to be produced. It was bis decree, that whichever succeeded in putting bis rival into this bag should obtain the hand of lus daughter. This singular encounter between the two gentlemen took place in the face of the whole Court. The contest lasted for more than an hour. At length the Spaniard yielded, and the German, Ehberhard, Baron de Taibert, having planted his rival in the bag, took it upon his back, and very gallantly laid it at the feet of his mistress, whom he espoused the next day. Such is the story, as gravely told by M. de St. Foix. It is impossible to say what the feelings of a successful combatant in a duel may be on his having passed a small sword through the body, or a bullet through the thorax, of his antagonist, but might be not quite as elated, and more conso- led, on having put his adversary "into a hag '" þÿ Table Talk.

TUB HEIRESS IN JEOPARDY. from " The. Blank Book of a small Colleger." How much of human hostility depends on hat circumstance þÿ distance! If the most bitpr enemies were to come in contact how fiucli their ideas of each other would be chast,ned and corrected ! They would mutually jmend their erroneous impressions ; see much o admire, and much to imitate in each other; jnd half the animosity that, sheds its baneful influence on society would fade away and be forgotten. It was one day when I was about seven vears old, after an unusual bustle in the family mansion, and my being arrayed in a black frock, much to my inconvenience, in the hot month of August, that I was told my asthmatic old uncle had gone oil' like a limb, and that I was heiress of ten thousand per annum. This information, given with an air of infinite importance, made no very great impression upon mc at the time ; and in spite of the circumstance being regtdarly dwelt on by my French governess at Camden House, after every henious misdemeanor, 1 had thought little or nothing on the subject, till at the age of eighteen 1 was called on to bid adieu to Fevizac and pirouettes, and hear my uncle's will read by my guardian. It furnished me, indeed, with ample materials for thinking. Mr. Marrowfat's face, neither human nor divine þÿ I see it before me while I am writing appeared positively þÿ frightful O as he recited its monstrous content. It appeared that my father and uncle, though brothers, had wrangled and jangled through life ; and that the only subject on which they

ever agreed was supporting the dignity of the Vavasour family; that in a moment of unprecedented unison, they had determined, that, as the title fell to my cousin Edgar, and the estates to me, to keep both united in the family, we should marry ; and it seemed, which ever party violated these previous conditions, was actually dependent on the other lor bread and butter. When I first heard of this arrangement, I blessed myself, and Sir Edgar cursed himself. A passionate, overbearing, desolute young man, thought 1, lor a husband þÿ for the husband of an orphan þÿ lor a girl who has not a nearer relation than himself in the world þÿ who has no father to advise her, no mother to support her : a professed rake, too, who will merely view me as an incumbrance on his estate, who will think no love, no contidence, no respect due to me ; who will insult my feelings, derive my sentiments, and wither with unkindness the best affections of my nature. No! 1 concluded, as my constitutional levity returned. I have the greatest possible respect for guardians, revere their office, and tremble at their authority ; but to make myself wretched merely to please them no, no \ 1 positively cannot think of it. Well Time, who is no respecter of persons, went on. The gentleman, who was within a few months of being twenty-one, and on the day of his attaining age, he was to say whether it was his pleasure to fulfil the engagement ; my opinion, I found, was not to be asked. A titled husband was procured for me,

and I was to take him and be thankful I was musing on niv singular situation, when a thought struck me : Can I not see him, and judge of his character unsuspected by himself? This is the season when he pays an annual nsit to my godmother ; why not persuado her

to let me visit her incog ? The dea, strange as it was, was constantly acted on, and a week saw me at Vale Royal, without carria- O ges, without horses, without servant; to all appearance, a girl of no pretensions or expectations, and avowedly dependent on a distant relation. To this hour I remember my heart beating audibly, as 1 descended to the dining room, where I was to see, for the first time, the future arbiter of my fate ; and I shall never forget my surprise when a pale, gentlemanly, and rather reserved young man, in apparent ill health, was introduced to me, for the noisysissolute, distracting, and distracted Baronet ! Preciously have 1 been hoaxed, thought 1, as after a long and' rather interesting conversa tion with Sir Edgar, 1 with the other ladies left the room. Days rolled on in succession Chance continually brought us together, and prudence began to whisper, You had belter " return home.' Still 1 lingered; till one evening, towards the close of a long tete-a-tete conversation, on my saying tnat I never considered money and happiness as synonymous terms, and thought it very possible to live on five hundred u-year, he replied. " One admission more : could you live on it with me ? ou are doubtless acquainted," he coutiiRied, with increasing emotion, with my unhappy situa- " tion ; but not perhaps aware, that, revolting lroin a union with Miss Vavasour, I have resolved on taking orders, and accepting a living troin a friend, if, foregoing more brilliant

prospects, you would condescend to share my retirement." His manner, the moment, the lovely scene which surrounded us, all combined against me, and heaven only knows what answer I might have been hurried into, had I not got out, with a gaiety foreign to my heart, " I can say nothing to you till you have, in person, explained your sentiments to Miss Vavasour. Nothing þÿ positively nothing" þÿ - " But why ? Can seeing her again and again," he returned, "ever reconcile me to her manners, habits, and sentiments, or any estates induce mc to place at the head of tny table a humpbacked has bleu, in green spectacles ?" " Humpbacked!" " Yes, from her cradle. þÿ But you color. Do you know her t" " Intimately. She's my most particular friend." þÿ " 1 sincerely beg your pardon What an unlucky dog I am ! 1 hope you're not offended (" " Ulfended ! offended ! oflended oh no, not ofleiided þÿ not the least offended. Humpbacked ! of all things in the world !" and 1 voluntarily gave a glance at the glass. " 1 had no conception," he resumed, as soon as he could collect himself, " that there was any acquaintance.' " Tle most intimate," 1 replied ; " anU I can assure you that vou have been represented to her as the most dissolute, passionate, awkward, ill disposed young man breathing." " Indeed ?" '"Yes, hear me. Bee your cousin V ou will find yourself mistaken. With her answer you shall have mine." And with a ludicrous attempt to smile, when I was monstrously inclined to cry, 1 contrived to

make my escape. We did not meet again ; for the next morning, in no very enviable frame of mind, I returned home. A few weeks afterwards Sir Edgar came of age. The bells were ringing bitterly in the breeze, the tenants were carousing on the lawn, when he drove up to the door. My cue was taken. With a large pair of green spectacles on my nose, in a darkened room, I prepared tor this tremendous interview. After hems and hahs innumerable, and with confusion the most distressing to himself, and the

The Begum Sumroo, (says Major Archer,) some days subsequent to her quitting the camp at Bhurtpore, in 1826 wrote to the commander in chief that she had no rest day nor night, since she had parted with him. þÿ His Excellency, in reply, said that "on his arrival at Cawnpore, he had found the boats which had been prepared for him high and dry, from the lowness of the river; but the tears he had shed when he thought of the period lie should be absent from her presence, had been so abundant as to float the vessels and enable him to proceed on his voyage." This was taken as a matter of course, and not considered otherwise than it should have been.

Wonders Have Not Ceased. þÿ On Thursday last, when the legal gentlemen had finished reading the indictment to James Miller, confined in Ayr jail f..r the murder of Ralph Wilson, as formerly announced in this paper, he unexpectedly, and to the astonishment of his hearers, began to þÿspeak after a continued silence of, we believe, nearly seventeen vears. His language is grammatically correct, in style superior to his sphere in life, and his discourse indicates that he had formerly read much on various subjects, chiefly political and historical. He acknowledges without hesitation having killed Wilson, and says he was warranted in doing so, in order to " put him out of pain his pains were produced, he declares, by taking magnesia : þÿ he gave him seven strokes with the hatchet, the first stroke being in the name and for the honour of the Queen. As usual with persons labouring under this sad malady, he assumes all the dignity of a great þÿpersonage calls himself Lord Waterside and Baron þÿCalcraft was the intimate friend of our late Kings George 3d and þÿ4th prime minister for four years to Louis the !8th of þÿFrance, that it was solely by bis manoeuvring that the Luke of Wellington gained the victory at Waterloo, þÿAc. But unfortunately for his greatness he was presented yesterday with a pair of new trousers, which were like Gilpin's borrowed wig; and hence he discovered his real craft, I y telling Mr. Kennedy, the jailer, that he could easily alter them to fit himself His bodily

health is obviously improved, and were we to hazard an opinion on the extraordinary departure of his taciturnity, we should say it might be the consequence of the muscles of hie tongue and parts connected w ith articulation becoming in like measure strengthened by the increase of his general þÿhealth. C HRISTIA NSTED, 13 th AUG. 1835. It is with sincere regret we ascertain that the very severe Gale which hinder'd the issuing of our Paper at the usual time, has occasioned considerable damage both in Town and Country þÿ which may be accounted for in consequence of its coming upon us in reality " like a thief in the night." On the evening of Wednesday the 12th inst , we hailed with joy the heavy showers of rain, which gave us promise of better things to come, enlivening our prospects for the following years' crop, which were hitherto cheerless through the previous long spell of dry weather; the Barometer giving no indications of the accompanying storm þÿ at midnight, however, the wind freshened considerably, and gradually put forth its energies until the dawn of day, when it swept over us with great and destructive fury þÿ tearing down fences and stone-walls, uprooting trees, unrooting and destroying houses, and only began to moderate at about 10 o'clock the following day.

Fortunately there were but few Vessels a Port, the names of which, together with the injury sustained, are as follows : þÿ Brig Bogota, of New-York, Capt. Clear, loaded and ready for sea, driven on shore, sustaining no damage, but the loss of masts and rigging, the Captain very promptly cutting the former for the preservation of Hull and Cargo. Brig Ottowa, of Philadelphia, Geo. Bishop Master, on shore. Brig Hercules, of New- York, W. B. Gardener, Master, also on shore. Both of these Vessels and their inward Cargoes have however, sustained no injury and can be got otf without damage either to llull or Rigging. Schooner Industry and Sloop Water Witch of this place, both on shore. Sloop St. Croix, sunk ; and two other small craft, on shore, and much injured. Thus far we are rejoiced to say the loss is not great, but when we elsewhere direct our attention, we find the visitation more severe. As within the brief space of the present division of our labours þÿ it were impossible to collect the necessary information of aii those who have suffered on this occasion, we for the present must content ourselves, with stating those which came under our immediate view. His Excellency the Governor General has sustained much loss at his Country Seat " Bulows Minde " whereat on the same day, the President of Venezuela His Excellency Dr. Vargas and Suite were festivally entertained, together with a numerous party, within brief space of whose departure, the violence of the wind demolished the splendid

and recently erected Dining-Room, valuable Furniture, Plate, Ac. The House on the Wharf, the property of G Gordon, Esq occupied by Mr Dauiilaro is partially unroofed, furniture much injured: þÿ In short, as before mentioned, it is at present out of our power to enter more fully into particulars, as but few, very few indeed have escaped unscathed. We had almost forgot to mention the safe arrival of the Government Packet Schooner Vigilant, which sailed from St. Thomas at 8 o'clock on the evening of the Gale; she entered the harbour at 1 o'clock and was enabled to ride out the storm, through the judicious manner in which she was moored, and the prudent vigilance of her Commander, Captain 1)ahl, (d. m.) We are without any advices from Fredorikstmd from whence the Man of War Brig St. Jan, Capt. Fischer, sailed on the evening of the Gale for the purpose of conveying His Excellency Dr. Vargas A Suite to Venezuela, we hope however, no serious damage may have happened, and that the Vessel will safely reacli her destined Port, as the wind was much in her favor.

Mnemonics þÿ Every time a certain artizan went to confess, he failed not to prepare himself for this act of devotion by beating his wife_ " What barbarity ! what cowardice I" said one of his neighbors to him, who had often been a hearer and spectator of this periodical broil. " Why do you beat a woman who, assuredly, is not worse than another ? You are a scandal to the whole neighbourhood 1' " Neighbor," said the unfeeling husband, " I have my reasons for acting as 1 do, and when they are known to you, I am sure you will approve of them, I have a very short memory, and do not recollect one fourth of my sins when 1 am on the point of going to confess, so that there remains for me but one way of remembering them, which is, to beat my wife, who then takes great care to recal them to my memory in the most glaring colors."

Haytian Paradise. þÿ Washington Irving observes, in his " Life of Columbus," that the Haytians had an idea of a place of reward, to which the spirits of good men repaired after death, where they were reunited to the spirits of those they had loved during life, and to all their ancestors. Here they enjoyed uninterruptedly, and in perfection, those pleasures which constituted their felicity on earth. þÿ They lived in shady and blooming bowers, with beautiful women, and banqueted on delicious fruits. The Paradise of these happy spirits was variously placed, almost every tribe assigning some favorite spot in their native province. Many, however, concurred in describing this region as being near a lake in the western part of the island, in the beautiful province of Xaiagua. Here there were delightful valeys, covered with a delicate fruit called the mamey, about the size of an apricot. They imagined that the souls of the deceased remained concealed among the airy and inaccessible cliffs of the mountains during the day but descended at night into these happy valleys, to regale on this consecrated fruit. The living were sparing, therefore, in eating of it, lest the souls of their friends should suffer from want of their favorite nourishment.

Wati:k-Proof Leather þÿ The following method of preparing water-proof leather at a very small expense, will he found invariably to succeed : þÿ Take one pint of drying oil, two ounces of yellow wax, two ounces of spirit of turpentine, and one ounce of burgundy pitch, melted carefully over a slow lire ; with this composition new shoes and boots are to be rubbed in the sun, or at a distance from the fire, with a sponge as often as they become dry, until they are fully saturated ; the leather then is impervious to wet, the shoes and boots last much longer, acquire softness and pliability, and thus prepared, are the most ellectual preservatives against cold and chilblains.

Mode of Trading at Shendy. þÿ The wholesale trade at Shendy principally conducted is through the agency of brokers A caravan no sooner arrives than every merchant's house is crowded with brokers; but the avidity and parsimony of all parties are too great to allow them to bring their transactions to a speedy conclusion. Even after the bargain is made, each party endeavours to cheat the other before the goods are delivered and the money paid. In addition to this, every attempt to enter into an engagement of any importance becomes known all over tiic place, and the jealousy of the traders often prevents its taking place. No merchandise has its fixed price ; there is no such thing as a price-current ; every one sells according to the prospect he has of cheating the buyer and bribing the broker. The purchase-money, or, in case of barter, its equivalent in merchandise, is almoft always immediately paid down. The longest credit I have witnessed is a couple of days; and it is evident, on the termination of every commercial transaction, that the buyer and seller reciprocally entertain suspicions of each other's honesty. To oblige a debtor to settle his accounts, recourse is generally had to the slaves of the Mek, who act as police-officers ; but a man who is unprotected and without friends is sure to lose the greater pari of Ins goods if he allows them to go out of his hands without immediate payment. þÿ BurckhardYs Travels in A ubia.
